lesson.title: Prophase: Chromosomes Condense, the Spindle Begins
lesson.summary: Prophase is the first stage of mitosis, when duplicated chromosomes condense into visible structures and the mitotic spindle begins to form as the nuclear envelope starts to break down.
lesson.body:
Prophase is the opening stage of mitosis, and its central job is preparation: getting the chromosomes and the cell's internal machinery ready for the physical work of separation that follows. At the start of prophase, the cell's DNA exists as chromatin, a loose, diffuse tangle that is efficient for gene expression but completely unworkable for moving chromosomes around without them getting tangled or broken. Prophase solves that problem by condensing the chromatin, coiling and packing the DNA of each chromosome, along with its associated proteins, into a tightly compacted, visibly distinct structure. Because DNA replication already happened back in S phase, each condensed chromosome at this point consists of two identical sister chromatids joined together at the centromere.

While the chromosomes are condensing, the cell is also building the machinery it will use to move them. In animal cells, the two centrosomes, which duplicated earlier in the cycle, begin migrating toward opposite ends, or poles, of the cell. As they move apart, each centrosome nucleates a radiating array of microtubules, and together these form the mitotic spindle. This is the cytoskeleton being actively repurposed, the same microtubule system that shapes and organizes the cell in interphase is disassembled and rebuilt here into a specialized structure with one job: capturing chromosomes.

Toward the end of prophase, the nuclear envelope, the membrane that has kept the chromosomes physically separated from the rest of the cell's interior, begins to break down, and the nucleolus disappears. This gives the spindle microtubules growing in from the centrosomes direct access to the chromosomes for the first time. Each chromosome has a specialized protein structure called a kinetochore located at its centromere, and as the nuclear envelope clears away, spindle microtubules begin capturing these kinetochores, setting the stage for the alignment that defines the next phase.
